passages.text: “But why,” he says, “if a man does not know that his own wife is committing adultery, does he not become jealous, grow angry, cause an uproar, or wage war? Thus such things are not evils by nature; rather, irrational human opinion makes them terrible.” But I say that, even if these terrible things do not happen, it is possible for the wife, through her intimacy with the adulterer, either to abandon her husband, or, even while living with him, to plot against him, or to give the adulterer what her husband acquired through toil. And while her husband is away, she may conceive by the adulterer and, because she is ashamed of being exposed, wish to destroy what is in her womb and become a child-killer, or, while destroying it, perish along with it. But if she conceives by an adulterer while her husband is living with her and then gives birth, the child, once reared, does not know his father but takes the man who is not his father to be his father. And so, when the man who is not his father dies, he leaves his own estate to someone else’s child. And how many other evils naturally tend to spring from adultery! We do not know the hidden things belonging to these evils. For just as a rabid dog kills those whom it touches by transmitting its utterly unseen rabies, so also the hidden evil of adultery, even when it remains unknown, brings about the severing of succession.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν μὴ τὰ δεινὰ ταῦτα συμβαίνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if these terrible things do not happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer particularly to the husband’s jealousy, anger, uproar, and conflict, or more generally to the harmful consequences just discussed; the English preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through her intimacy with the adulterer
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθεια can denote familiarity, association, or intimacy; the adulterous context supports “intimacy,” while the wife remains the understood subject of the following infinitives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to destroy what is in her womb
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom τὸ κατὰ γαστρός denotes what is in the womb. “Destroy” preserves φθείρω without replacing the author’s wording with a modern technical term.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he leaves his own estate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here βίος most naturally means one’s means of living or property left at death, rather than biological life; “livelihood” or “possessions” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the severing of succession
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαδοχή may denote succession, inheritance, or continuation of a family line. The context of misidentified paternity and inheritance favors “succession” while leaving the precise dimension open.

source_issues.issue: The printed form has unassimilated συν- before φ. It remains intelligible as an orthographic form of the compound meaning “to be destroyed together,” so no content is uncertain.

The prefixed hyphen is present in the supplied image-checked reading but has no evident syntactic or morphological function. It is provisionally treated as a typographical feature rather than as part of the noun.

passages.text: But let that now be passed over by us. This, however, we all know: as a rule, men are uncontrollably indignant over it; wars have been stirred up over it, households have been overthrown, cities have been captured, and countless other things have occurred. For this reason I took refuge with the Jews’ holy God and their law, having placed my confidence in the firm judgment that, from God’s just judgment, both law has been laid down and the soul, wherever it may be, certainly receives what its deeds deserve.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression indicates what happens generally or for the most part, not an exceptionless claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are uncontrollably indignant
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεπισχέτως conveys lack of restraint, while δυσχεραίνω can mean to be displeased, distressed, or indignant; the ensuing wars and destruction support the stronger contextual wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδεδωκὼς τὴν πίστιν ἀσφαλεῖ τῇ κρίσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: having placed my confidence in the firm judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πίστις here denotes confidence or credence given to a conclusion. An alternative is “having entrusted my faith to the sure judgment,” but that can suggest a more technical religious use than the construction requires.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what its deeds deserve
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the soul receives “what is according to the worth of the things it did”; the rendering expresses proportionate recompense without specifying reward or punishment beyond the Greek.

passages.text:
After I said this, Appion added to the argument, saying, “What then? Do not the laws of the Greeks also forbid base acts and punish adulterers?”

I said, “Then the gods of the Greeks, since they have acted contrary to the laws, owe a penalty. Moreover, how will I be able to discipline myself if I suppose that the gods themselves were the first to commit every grievous act along with adultery and have paid no penalty, although they owe it all the more for this very reason, since they are not enslaved to desire? But if they were subject to it, how could they be gods?”

Appion said, “Then let our objects of attention no longer be gods, but the judges; with our eyes on them, we will be afraid to sin.”

I replied, “The cases are not alike, Appion. A person who keeps a human being in view will dare to sin in the hope of escaping notice. But one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything, knowing that he cannot escape God’s notice, will refrain even from sinning in secret.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: added to the argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression means to bring or add something to the ongoing discourse; “responded to the argument” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they owe it all the more for this very reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: ταύτῃ points forward to their not being enslaved to desire: freedom from compulsion makes the gods, on the speaker’s reasoning, more accountable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let our objects of attention be
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκοποί can mean goals, marks, or objects kept in view. The following εἰς οὓς ἀφορῶντες supports the visual and exemplary sense rather than “goals” alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν παντεπόπτην τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ ὁρισάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction can be rendered more formally as “one who has defined God in his soul as all-seeing.” The chosen wording gives a defensible modern English expression of the internal conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will refrain even from sinning in secret
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραιτέομαι here means to decline, avoid, or refrain from an action; καί adds the force “even” in context.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between πῶς and the postpositive δέ. That punctuation interrupts what is otherwise a coherent question, so the translation provisionally construes the words together without altering the supplied Greek wording.

passages.text:
When Appion heard this, he said, “Ever since I heard that you were associating with Jews, I knew that your outlook had changed. For someone has aptly said, ‘Bad associations corrupt good character.’”

I replied, “Then good associations correct worthless character.”

Appion said, “Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first. But tomorrow—here, if it pleases you—when the same friends have assembled, I will demonstrate that our gods are neither adulterers nor murderers nor destroyers of children, and that they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters. Rather, the ancients, wishing only lovers of learning to know the mysteries, veiled them in myths of the kind you have described. For in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance, Cronus is time, and Rhea is the ever-flowing nature of water. Nevertheless, as I promised, tomorrow at dawn, when you have assembled, I will interpret each particular form allegorically and reveal to you the truth about what exists.”

In response I said, “Tomorrow do just as you have promised. But now, beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: your outlook had changed
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη can denote mind, judgment, opinion, or outlook. The passive ἠλλοιῶσθαι indicates that it had been altered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Bad associations corrupt good character
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμιλίαι denotes associations or company, and ἤθη denotes habits, morals, or character. The wording preserves the maxim and its reversal in the next sentence without making a familiar rendering from another work controlling.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Σήμερον πεπληροφορήμην τὴν σὴν ἐπιγνῶναι ἔνστασιν, διὸ σοὶ πρώτῳ εἰπεῖν συνεχωρήσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pluperfect πεπληροφορήμην places the settled resolve before the permission expressed by συνεχωρήσαμεν, while ἐπιγνῶναι can denote learning or ascertaining the position. This sequence favors a prospective reading: Appion had resolved to ascertain the position and therefore let the other speaker go first. A materially possible alternative is “Today I had become fully assured that I understood your objection,” taking πεπληροφορήμην as achieved assurance and ἐπιγνῶναι as recognition already attained; ἔνστασις may mean “objection,” “position,” or “contention.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destroyers of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: φθορεύς can denote a destroyer or corrupter. In a list with adultery and murder and in the context of myths about the gods, “destroyers” is the more direct choice, though “corrupters of children” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλησιάζω literally means to approach or associate closely, but with these dative objects and the surrounding accusations of sexual misconduct it has a sexual sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ζῆνα γὰρ τὴν ζέουσαν οὐσίαν εἶναι φυσιολογοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυσιολογοῦσιν introduces a natural-philosophical explanation. The Greek also makes an etymological sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν that cannot be reproduced naturally in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: each particular form
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer to each divine figure, each mythic form, or each individual feature of the allegory. “Form” preserves the expression without selecting one referent too narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐντεῦθεν καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἃ μέλλεις λέγειν, ἄκουσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek elliptically commands Appion to hear something directed toward or bearing upon his forthcoming claims. “Listen to a reply to the very things you are going to say” is another possible way to supply the English relation.

passages.text:
If the deeds of the gods, though good, were veiled in evil myths, great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them, because he hid honorable things beneath evil narratives so that no one might become an imitator of them. But if they truly committed impious acts, those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives, so that people, looking up to them as their superiors, would not attempt sins like theirs.

After I said this, those present were plainly beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made. Indeed, after repeatedly and earnestly urging me to come without fail on the following day, they departed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies the person responsible for concealing the deeds; “is demonstrated on the part of the one who covered them” is a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honorable things
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεμνός can mean venerable, august, solemn, or honorable. Here it describes supposedly good divine deeds that would merit imitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπειν is understood here in the sense of covering over, corresponding to the earlier language of veiling. The substantival ἀγαθοῖς takes its contextual content from the preceding “myths” and “narratives.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: looking up to them as their superiors
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττονας may mean those who are better, stronger, or superior. The gods function here as supposedly higher examples whom humans observe and imitate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνοντες τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνειν with the genitive means to make a beginning of something. λόγοι may be words, statements, or arguments; the argumentative setting favors “arguments,” while the printed middle dot is provisionally treated as editorial punctuation that does not prevent ἀγάπης from completing the construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me to come without fail on the following day
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως expresses insistence that the visit occur in any event or by all means.

source_issues.source_quote: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between λόγους and ἀγάπης, although the surrounding words support the continuous genitive construction “love for the arguments spoken by me.” The translation provisionally adopts that defensible syntax while preserving disclosure of the printed punctuation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους ἀγάπης
